paragraphs: The strongest case against returning museum objects to their places of origin is not the ugly one. It is not the claim that the objects were lawfully acquired, which is often false and in any event a matter for lawyers. It is the universalist case: that certain objects belong to everyone rather than to any single people, and that a great collection assembled in one city lets a visitor set a bronze head beside a marble figure made two thousand miles away and learn something neither object teaches alone. I think this premise is true. I want to show that it does not support the conclusion it is used to defend.

Grant, then, that an object's meaning is enlarged by comparison, and that humanity is the proper audience for it. Ask who is thereby entitled to the comparison. On the universalist premise the answer cannot be the residents of the few capitals where the collections happen to sit. Humanity is distributed, and a premise about humanity is an argument about access. Access is poorly served by concentration. The premise therefore tells against the present arrangement more sharply than any argument from ownership does, and it has the advantage of not depending on who the rightful owner is.

The usual reply is practical. Objects are fragile, conservation is expensive, and the institutions that can guarantee it are, as it happens, the ones already holding the objects. This is a real consideration and a shrinking one; but notice what has happened to the argument. It has stopped defending the universal museum and started defending a particular museum's present capacity, which is a contingent fact about budgets. An argument from the universality of art cannot in the end rest on the durability of an air-conditioning plant.

A better reply concedes the point about distribution and insists that something is still lost by dispersal. A collection is not an aggregate of objects but a structure, and much of its value lies in the adjacencies. I accept this, and it changes less than it appears to. Adjacency is a choice, and the adjacencies of the great collections were not designed by anyone. They are the residue of what expeditions happened to bring back and what trade routes happened to carry. A structure assembled by the history of acquisition is not thereby the structure that best teaches, and treating it as untouchable confuses an inheritance with an argument.

What the premise actually requires is that objects circulate, and that the institutions which lend should not always be the same institutions which hold. Nothing in the universalist case picks out permanent retention by the present holder; the case picks out whatever arrangement puts the most people in a position to compare. Repatriation, on this view, is neither a penalty nor an act of atonement. It is a redistribution of the capacity to compare, and the universalist should want it for reasons of his own.

There is a cost I do not want to minimise. A returned object may be displayed to a narrower purpose than the universalist wants: as evidence of a nation rather than as an object of attention. The risk is real, and it is symmetrical. The universal museum has a narrowing of its own, which is to display an object as an instance of a category it never belonged to, under a label written in a language its makers did not speak. Nothing in the argument guarantees good custodians anywhere. It settles only who, on the universalist's own premise, should be given the chance to be one.

For most of the last century the economics of education rested on a single sentence which was in fact two claims fastened together: schooling makes people more productive, and that is why the schooled are paid more. The first is a claim about what happens to a student. The second is a claim about what an employer is buying. Nothing distinguished them in the available data, so the sentence served. A series of findings has now pulled the two apart, and much current confusion comes from treating evidence against one as evidence against the other.

The findings concern the shape of the earnings curve. Earnings rise sharply at the completion of a credential rather than smoothly with time spent studying. Students who finish three years of a four-year programme and leave earn far closer to those who never enrolled than to graduates, although they have sat through three quarters of the instruction. Where a leaving certificate is awarded by examination, measured earnings jump at the pass mark: candidates one point below the cut and one point above it have received the same teaching for the same number of years, and are paid differently for decades. If pay tracked what had been learned, discontinuities of this kind would not appear.

The natural reading is that the credential is a signal. It is cheaper for the capable to obtain, and therefore informative to an employer who cannot observe capability directly and must sort applicants somehow. The signalling account predicts the discontinuities, which no account built on accumulated instruction can do. But here the two claims must be held apart rather than one put in place of the other. Evidence that pay does not track learning is not evidence that schooling does not teach. Those are separate questions, and the discontinuity findings bear on only the first.

On the second question the evidence runs the other way. Studies that measure what students can do, rather than what they are later paid, find gains that are real and uneven. Where years of schooling were changed by law rather than by the student's choice, measured literacy and numeracy rise with the additional years, and they rise for students who left without a certificate as well as for those who stayed to collect one. Something was acquired by the three-year leaver. What was not acquired was the document.

Holding the claims apart changes which policies make sense. If pay follows learning, enlarging the supply of instruction raises wages. If pay follows the signal, enlarging the supply of credentials mostly raises the level at which the signal is set, and each cohort must go further than the last to say the same thing about itself. The second prediction is the one the figures have kept confirming: the share of advertised posts requiring a degree has risen faster than any measured change in what those posts involve. A private return can stay high while the social return falls, which is what one expects if part of what is purchased is position.

None of this shows that instruction is wasted, or that the signal is arbitrary; a signal no capability underwrote would stop being informative, and employers would stop paying for it. The useful statement is narrower. A degree does two things at once, and no measurement that reports a single figure for the value of a degree has yet distinguished them. Until a study separates them, the quarrel between those who call higher education an investment and those who call it a sorting device will go on being conducted with numbers neither side is entitled to.

We use the word child as though it named a stage of life the way adult names a condition: a natural fact any society must have noticed and made provision for. The provisions differ, we assume, but not the thing provided for. The assumption is worth tracing, because the category has a history, and the history is shorter than the assumption implies.

The claim is not that earlier societies failed to love their young, which is both false and beside the point. It is a claim about the category: what counts as a child, where the line falls, and what it is for. Household inventories and parish records of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries describe the young by what they could do. Could they carry, tend animals, read, be bound to a trade? The vocabulary of those documents groups a nine-year-old who worked beside the workers with the adults, and leaves a nineteen-year-old apprentice who kept no household of his own among the dependants. Years lived mattered less than capacity and station, and no single word in those records does the work our word does.

Three developments assembled the modern category, none of them intending it. Schooling came to gather pupils by year of birth, because a graded class needs cohorts; once the cohort existed, age became the salient fact about a person, and a departure from the age-norm became something to diagnose. The regulation of labour then drew its line at an age rather than at a capacity, because an age could be read off a register while a capacity had to be judged; the line then had to be given a meaning, which the schoolroom already standing on the other side of it supplied. Finally the collection of vital records made age a thing the state knew about everybody, and what a state can count it tends to govern by.

A genealogy of this kind is often read as a debunking, and it should not be. Showing that a category was assembled does not show that it is false, or that we would do better without it. Childhood, once built, acquired real content: the protections are not fictions, and the developmental differences the schools went on to discover are not artefacts of the registers that first sorted the pupils. What it shows is narrower and sharper. It shows that the category carries the shape of the instruments which made it: thresholds at round ages, an expectation of uniformity within a year group, and a habit of identifying the young by what they cannot yet do rather than by what they can.

The shape shows in the difficulties the category now has. Where a young person's capacities and their age disagree, our institutions are obliged to treat the age as the fact and the capacity as the anomaly. The disputes cluster exactly where one would expect them to cluster if the line had been drawn by registers rather than by anything about the young: at the thresholds, and in the cases where what someone can do is not what their year of birth predicts.

No programme follows from this. A category with such a history is not replaceable on that account, and no society that keeps registers will stop governing by age; the alternative, judging capacity case by case, is the thing the registers were adopted to avoid. The modest conclusion is worth holding. When childhood is invoked as the natural measure against which some arrangement is to be judged, we are using as a standard something that was made, recently, by particular instruments, for purposes of their own.

The standard account of assimilation runs in one direction. Newcomers arrive with practices, a language and attachments formed elsewhere; over time, and more thoroughly in the second generation, they take on those of the receiving society; and the degree to which they do so explains how well they come to be received. Acceptance is the dependent variable and adaptation the independent one. Policy built on this account addresses itself to the migrant, through language classes, civic instruction and tests.

The arrow can be run the other way, and when it is, findings that sit awkwardly in the standard account fall into place. Measured rates of intermarriage, residential dispersal and language shift vary far more across receiving regions than across countries of origin. Groups from a single origin, arriving in the same decade, converge at very different rates depending on where they settled; groups from different origins settled in the same place converge at similar rates. If adaptation were doing the explaining, the pattern would be the other way about.

Two further findings point the same way. Audit studies, which send employers applications identical but for the name at the top, report penalties that do not diminish for applicants whose records show local schooling from the first year to the last. The markers of adaptation, in other words, do not purchase acceptance. Second, longitudinal surveys find that reported belonging falls between the first generation and the second in some settings and rises in others. The second generation is more adapted everywhere, so adaptation cannot account for a difference in sign; what differs is what the second generation met when it presented itself as a member.

The inversion is this. Acceptance is not the reward for assimilation; what we call assimilation is largely the record of acceptance already granted. Where institutions admit newcomers to ordinary membership, in housing, in employment, in schools attended by everyone else's children, the practices that mark difference lose their function and fall away without anyone being instructed. Where admission is withheld, the same practices acquire a function they did not have before: they become the materials of a membership that is available when the other is not.

The obvious objection is that some groups keep their practices under conditions of full admission. Religious communities that hold to endogamy and to schools of their own, while facing no measurable penalty in employment or housing, are the standing example, and the inverted account must not predict that difference always dissolves. It does not. What it predicts is that persistence under admission will look unlike persistence under exclusion: selective rather than general, avowed rather than defensive, and unaccompanied by withdrawal from common institutions. The surveys bear this out, and the two kinds of persistence separate cleanly on measures of civic participation.

A caution about the evidence is owed. Receiving regions differ in many ways besides their openness, and the comparison of same-origin groups across regions is the strongest design available rather than an experiment; a region that admits newcomers readily may also be the region whose labour market was expanding when they arrived. The practical upshot is not that instruction for newcomers is useless, since a language is worth having whatever it buys. It is that a programme addressed only to the newcomer has mistaken the dependent variable for the independent one, and will go on being puzzled by its own results.

A critic who writes that a performance was shallow has said something, and it is surprisingly hard to say what. The sentence has the form of a report, yet nothing in the hall could have been measured to confirm it. One wants an account of what makes a judgement of this kind true, or at least answerable. The candidates present themselves in a natural order, and each fails in a way that prepares the next.

The first is that the judgement reports the critic's pleasure. It does not. A critic may be bored by a performance she judges superb and gripped by one she judges cheap, and in saying both she contradicts herself in no way at all; the two sentences are about different things. There is a further difficulty. A report of pleasure invites agreement or its absence and nothing more, whereas a critical judgement invites the thing criticism is for, which is disagreement that goes somewhere. Nobody argues anyone out of a sensation.

The second candidate is that the judgement reports a consensus, actual or eventual: what competent listeners do or will come to agree about. This fails on a case the history of performance supplies in quantity. A critic who dissents from every competent listener of her generation is not thereby mistaken, and the records show reputations rising and falling without anyone having learned a new fact. Consensus is evidence about a judgement of this kind. It is not what the judgement is about, and treating it as such leaves us unable to say what the dissenter and the majority are disagreeing over.

The third candidate looks sturdier: the judgement applies rules, a standard of execution, fidelity to the written text, balance between the parts. Rules of this kind are either coarse enough to be satisfied by performances nobody admires, or they have been derived backwards from performances already admired, in which case they summarise a judgement rather than grounding one. And the cases criticism finds most interesting are those in which a rule is broken to effect, which a rule cannot itself license.

What survives the eliminations is this. A judgement of the kind we are examining claims that the performance rewards a certain way of listening, and it is answerable in the way directions are answerable, by being followed. Shallow says that an attention which goes looking for structure here will find the surface and nothing under it. A critic who says it incurs an obligation to say where to listen, which is why good criticism is full of instructions, this passage, this transition, this refusal to slow down, and why a review that offers a verdict and no route is not doing the thing even when its verdict is the one we would give.

It may be objected that this makes criticism a report about listeners after all, merely a different report. The difference is the whole point. A claim about what rewards attention is a claim about what is there to be found, and it can fail as a direction fails: you follow it and the thing is not there. Taste, on this account, is not a preference one happens to have but a practice one can be better or worse at, and the long disputes about taste are not disputes about sensation. They are disagreements about where to look, conducted between people who can take each other to the place.

Studies of how people estimate hazards return a consistent set of results. Asked to rank causes of death, respondents overstate the rare and dramatic and understate the common and chronic. Willingness to pay for protection responds more to the vividness of a described loss than to its stated probability. Demand for flood coverage rises after a flood and lapses over the following years at a rate that tracks nothing about the floodplain. Offered coverage against a small loss at a premium above the expected value of what is covered, a clear majority take it.

Set beside these findings is the arithmetic of insurance, which is not in dispute. A premium is an expected loss plus the cost of carrying it. Pooling works because independent risks aggregate predictably, so that a company which cannot say which house will burn can say with precision how many will. An insurer that priced to perceptions rather than to frequencies would be insolvent within a few years, and the frequencies are not a matter of opinion.

The conclusion the evidence invites is that lay judgement of risk is an error to be corrected: that the actuary supplies the right number, and the task of policy is to bring the public's choices into line with it. I have taught these findings for twenty years and I no longer draw that conclusion. The reason is not that the findings are weak. It is that the quantity people are responding to is not the quantity the calculation produces, and the mismatch is not always a mistake.

An expected value is a statement about a population of events. A household faces one draw. A loss that is modest in expectation may be unrecoverable in fact, and the figure that matters to a family is not what the average flood costs but whether this flood ends their ability to go on; the two come apart precisely for the low-probability, high-severity events on which the literature concentrates. So the findings lump together two judgements that ought to be kept separate. Paying a loading to insure a loss one could absorb out of savings is irrational on any reading. Declining to treat one's own exposure as an average is not.

What of vividness and recency? These are harder to defend and I do not defend them entirely. But consider what a recent flood supplies which a published frequency does not: information about local particulars, where the water went, which drains failed, whether the defences held and for how long. No table of base rates contains any of it. Responding to an event is a poor way to estimate a probability and a decent way to read a situation, and some of what is scored as recency bias is a response to the only local evidence a household has.

The corrective programme therefore wants reorganising rather than abandoning. The errors worth attacking are the ones that survive the distinction: over-insuring the absorbable, under-insuring the ruinous, and above all the lapse of coverage in the quiet years after an event, which nothing in the foregoing defends and which leaves households exposed exactly as the memory of why they bought the policy fades. What should not be attacked is the public's refusal to treat its own exposure as an average. That refusal is not a failure to grasp the arithmetic. It is a correct view about whose arithmetic it is.

Every map of a sphere on a plane distorts, and the first thing a cartography student learns is the tariff: a projection may preserve angles or areas but not both, and which it preserves is a decision. The lesson is usually drawn as a caution about honesty: the mapmaker should declare the projection, the reader should ask. Stated that way, the lesson treats distortion as a tax on an otherwise straightforward description, and leaves the harder question untouched. What is a map answerable to?

The question is best approached through a case where the usual answer gives no help. Take a river that moves. A mapped channel is correct for a season; the water then cuts a new course and abandons the old, sometimes in a single flood, and the line on the sheet now describes a dry bed. The case is hard because every answer to the question which line is right can be defended: the channel as surveyed, the channel as it stands today, the envelope within which it has wandered for a century, the axis of the valley it will not leave. These are not four competing estimates of one quantity. They are four different quantities, each the right one for a different question: a boundary dispute, a bridge, a flood plan, an account of how the valley was cut.

The hard case generalises. It shows that the cartographer's choice is prior to accuracy rather than derived from it, because accuracy is a relation between a map and a question, and a map cannot be checked until the question it answers has been fixed. Projection is the famous such choice, not the deepest. Deeper are the decisions about what counts as a thing: whether a settlement of three hundred is a place, whether a track is a road, whether the river is a line or a band.

It will be objected that this makes all maps equally good, each right for its own question. The hard case shows why not. The defensible answers for the river are few, and a map that drew the channel where the water has never run would be wrong on every one of them. A map can also be convicted of a second fault: answering a question it conceals. When a single-line channel is printed on a sheet used for settling boundaries, it asserts a stability that nobody who surveyed it believed in. The charge is not inaccuracy but misdirection: the map answers a question other than the one its use requires, and says nothing about the substitution.

This reframes what disclosure is for. A note naming the projection is a start, and on its own tells a reader little. What a reader needs is the question, and some traditions supply it unasked. A nautical chart announces its question in its omissions: lavish about depths on the approach, almost silent about what lies inland of the shore, and no one takes the blank interior for a claim that nothing is there. The chart is honest not because it declares its projection but because its purpose is legible in what it leaves out.

The cartographer's choices are not a regrettable residue of working on paper. They are the acts that make a map a map rather than an inventory, and a sheet that hid them would be no more objective, only harder to use. The reader's obligation is to know what they are holding. A sheet that leaves its question obscure fails in the way a confident witness fails who has never been asked what they were in a position to see.

The long argument about gifts has been conducted as an argument about motives. One side holds that a gift is a disguised transaction: the giver anticipates a return, and his denial of it is part of the mechanism. The other holds that a gift is unlike a sale, since the giver asks for nothing and the recipient owes nothing enforceable. Both sides agree about where the question lies, which is inside the people involved. That agreement is the error.

Begin with why motive is the wrong place to look. In experimental work, giving is barely altered by manipulations that ought to move a calculating giver, and strongly altered by manipulations of form. Whether a transfer is entered in a ledger, whether it is made in cash or in kind, whether it is handed over in the presence of others: these change both rates of giving and rates of return, while information about the likelihood of a future return changes them much less. Respondents who describe their giving in frankly instrumental terms give in the same patterns as those who call it pure generosity. Whatever motives are doing, they are not doing the explaining.

So move the question. It is not about what a giver wants but about what the form of a transfer creates. A sale closes: once the price is paid the parties are quits. A gift does not close, and this is a fact about the institution rather than about anyone's intentions. The recipient is left with something that is not a debt, since there is no sum, no date and no enforcement, and yet is not nothing: a standing in a relationship which further transfers express. Cash entered in a ledger converts a gift into a sale precisely because a ledger closes an account.

The relocation dissolves a puzzle motive-talk cannot handle. Why is it offensive to name the return one expects? On the transaction view that is mere candour; on the generosity view it is irrelevant. On the present view the answer is structural: to name the return is to propose a closing, and so to propose that the relationship the gift opened be settled and brought to an end. The same account explains asymmetries that look like etiquette. Repayment that is exact and prompt is received as a rebuff, and the ethnographic record is full of rules that make closure difficult: delay, inexactness, objects that may never be sold.

There are gifts that are plainly transactions, the supplier's present at contract time. The point is not that no transfer is calculated, but that participants themselves identify these cases by the structural criterion rather than by reading minds. We do not say the lobbyist's gift was improper because we know what he was thinking; it was improper because it opened an obligation inside a relationship that is supposed to be closed: an office is meant to be quits with everyone it deals with.

The same test marks out the limits of exchange. The transfers a society refuses to let be bought tend to be the ones whose giving is not supposed to close. A kidney given and a kidney bought may be the same organ, and the objection to the market is not that the seller's motive is base, but that a sale leaves the parties quits, and this transfer is not supposed to leave anybody quits. Whether that is a good enough reason to forbid the sale is a further question, which nothing here settles. But it is at least the right question, which an argument about motives could never reach.

Writers are often praised for what they leave out, and the praise is usually made intelligible by an analogy with music. A rest in a score is not an absence of music but a notated part of it, with a duration, a place in the metre and a function; it belongs to the piece as the notes do. Carry it across and a literary omission becomes an element of the work: the scene not shown, the motive never stated, the twenty years a chapter break passes over in a clause. The analogy is good, and worth pressing, because the point at which it fails is where the subject becomes interesting.

Press it first on its strength. The music case establishes that an absence can be structural rather than deficient, and supplies a criterion: a rest has a duration one can count. A narrative that has moved at the pace of an afternoon a chapter and then crosses two decades in a clause has produced a gap of a definite size, which readers feel as a shape rather than a lack of information. Where the surrounding text has established a rhythm of disclosure, the thing not disclosed occupies a place that can be located precisely.

Now the break, which comes in three places. A rest is heard by everyone in the hall at the same moment; nobody mistakes it for the end of the piece, and nobody fills it with notes of their own. An omission is unlike this, first, in not being perceptible as an omission to a reader who has not registered the rhythm it departs from; second, in being filled, since a reader who meets an unstated motive does not experience a gap but supplies a motive, usually without noticing, and different readers supply different ones; and third, in not being identifiable from the work alone. A page is silent about almost everything, the colour of the walls, the weather in the next county; what makes one silence an omission rather than mere unmention is that the text has taught us to expect the thing.

The analogy breaks on expectation, and the break yields the account. An omission is not an element of the text but a relation between the text and an expectation the text has formed in a reader; the writer's material is not silence but the expectations that make a silence audible. This explains why the technique fails in two opposite ways. A rest can be played badly but cannot fail to be a rest, whereas an omission whose expectation was never established is simply a thing not mentioned, and no significance intended by the writer will make it heard. The opposite failure belongs to readers who arrive with expectations the text did not build, and hear withheld meaning everywhere.

It might be objected that this dissolves the writer's art into the reader's. It does not: the expectation is the writer's work, built sentence by sentence, and capable of being done well or badly, and a text that has established no rhythm of disclosure will not produce the experience in any reader, however willing. What the account denies is that the omission can be inspected on its own, as a rest can be found in a bar.

The much-praised restraint is the conspicuous half of a technique whose real work was done earlier, in building the expectation the restraint then disappoints. Our critical vocabulary has this the wrong way round, treating the withheld scene as the achievement. The achievement is the pages that make its absence a presence, and those pages are usually full.

questions.stem: The central claim of the passage is that:

choices.A: museums have no legitimate claim to objects that were acquired by expeditions and trade
choices.B: the practical obstacles to returning objects are smaller than defenders of museums admit
choices.C: objects acquired abroad should be displayed as evidence of the nations that produced them
choices.D: the universalist defence of great collections argues for returning objects, not for keeping them

questions.explanation: The author states his project in the first paragraph: the universalist premise 'is true' but 'does not support the conclusion it is used to defend', and the fifth paragraph draws the conclusion that repatriation is 'a redistribution of the capacity to compare' that 'the universalist should want'.

wrong.A: The question of lawful acquisition is set aside in the opening paragraph as 'a matter for lawyers', and the argument is built without any claim about ownership.
wrong.B: Conservation costs are handled in one paragraph as a reply that defends a particular museum's budget rather than the universal museum, not as the thesis.
wrong.C: The final paragraph names national display as a real cost of return, so it is something the author concedes against his conclusion, not something he recommends.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the universalist case for great collections rests on the idea that:

choices.A: the nations of origin have usually failed to care for comparable objects
choices.B: the law of acquisition was settled at the time the collections were formed
choices.C: objects of this kind are too fragile to be moved between institutions safely
choices.D: an object's meaning grows when it can be compared with distant objects

questions.explanation: The first paragraph gives the case as the claim that a collection in one city lets a visitor set objects from distant places side by side and 'learn something neither object teaches alone'; the second restates the granted premise as the claim that meaning 'is enlarged by comparison'.

wrong.A: No comparison of custodians appears in the universalist case; the final paragraph says instead that nothing 'guarantees good custodians anywhere'.
wrong.B: Legality is explicitly set aside at the start as 'often false and in any event a matter for lawyers', which is why the author does not argue from it.
wrong.C: Fragility is introduced later as the practical reply, and the author distinguishes it from the universalist case it is offered in support of.

questions.stem: The author mentions the durability of an air-conditioning plant in order to:

choices.A: concede that conservation standards are the decisive consideration in such disputes
choices.B: illustrate how much the cost of caring for fragile objects has fallen in recent years
choices.C: show that the practical reply has quietly changed what it is defending
choices.D: suggest that museums exaggerate the fragility of the objects they hold

questions.explanation: The paragraph says of the practical reply that it 'has stopped defending the universal museum and started defending a particular museum's present capacity, which is a contingent fact about budgets'; the plant is the image for that contingent fact.

wrong.A: The author calls conservation 'a real consideration and a shrinking one', which is the opposite of treating it as decisive.
wrong.B: Costs are called shrinking in a single clause, and no figures or trends are offered; the work of the passage is done by the shift in what is being defended.
wrong.D: The passage never disputes that the objects are fragile; it disputes what follows from that fact for the universalist argument.

questions.stem: The author's response to the argument from adjacency suggests that he regards the layout of existing great collections as:

choices.A: a scholarly achievement that could not be reproduced elsewhere
choices.B: a deliberate design whose teaching purpose has since been lost
choices.C: an accident of collecting that carries no authority of its own
choices.D: an arrangement too valuable to be altered for the sake of access

questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says the adjacencies 'were not designed by anyone' but are 'the residue of what expeditions happened to bring back', and that treating such a structure as untouchable 'confuses an inheritance with an argument'.

wrong.A: The author grants that adjacency has value but denies the arrangement is an achievement, since he says nobody designed it.
wrong.B: A lost design would still have been a design; the passage's point is that there was none to lose.
wrong.D: This is the position the author is answering, and he says explicitly that the consideration 'changes less than it appears to'.

questions.stem: A museum announces that it will keep its collection intact but send a third of it abroad each year on long rotating loans. The author would most likely regard this policy as:

choices.A: inadequate, because the objects would remain under a label written in a foreign language
choices.B: misguided, because the loans would subject fragile objects to avoidable risks of damage
choices.C: unnecessary, because the universalist premise is satisfied by a single great collection
choices.D: responsive to his argument, though short of the change in holding that he urges

questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph asks for two things: that objects 'circulate', which the policy does, and that 'the institutions which lend should not always be the same institutions which hold', which a policy of keeping the collection intact does not.

wrong.A: The foreign label is raised in the last paragraph as one narrowing among two, not as a standard the author applies to lending schemes.
wrong.B: Damage in transit is never offered as an objection by this author; fragility appears only in the reply he is criticising.
wrong.C: This is the view the whole passage attacks: concentration is said to serve the universal audience badly.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's argument?

choices.A: Several nations of origin have declined objects that were offered back to them on loan
choices.B: A comparison of the kind the universalist describes requires one institution to hold objects by the thousand
choices.C: Conservation at institutions outside the capitals still costs more than it does inside them
choices.D: The great collections were assembled with no plan for teaching anyone by comparison

questions.explanation: The argument turns on the step that 'Access is poorly served by concentration', and so that the capacity to compare can be redistributed. If comparison required a single holding of thousands of objects, concentration would be the only way to supply what the universalist premise values.

wrong.A: The author's claim is about who should be given 'the chance to be one' of the custodians, which a declined offer leaves untouched.
wrong.C: Costs of this kind are dismissed in the third paragraph as 'a contingent fact about budgets' rather than a defence of the universal museum.
wrong.D: This is the author's own point in the fourth paragraph, where the adjacencies are called the residue of what expeditions brought back.

questions.stem: The passage is primarily concerned with:

choices.A: demonstrating that the earnings advantage of graduates has been overstated
choices.B: arguing that employers would sort applicants better with other information
choices.C: distinguishing two claims about degrees that have long been treated as one
choices.D: tracing the rise in the share of posts that now require a degree

questions.explanation: The first paragraph identifies the two claims fastened into one sentence, one 'about what happens to a student' and one 'about what an employer is buying', and the last paragraph restates the thesis: 'A degree does two things at once, and no measurement that reports a single figure for the value of a degree has yet distinguished them.'

wrong.A: The graduate earnings advantage is reported as real throughout; what is disputed is what explains it, not its size.
wrong.B: Employers appear only as agents who 'must sort applicants somehow', and no better instrument for sorting is proposed.
wrong.D: That trend is cited once in the fifth paragraph as support for one prediction, not as the subject of the passage.

questions.stem: The passage presents the earnings gap between candidates just above and just below an examination cut as evidence that:

choices.A: examinations of this kind measure capability more accurately than coursework
choices.B: employers have little information about what any given school teaches
choices.C: pay is not determined by the amount of instruction a candidate received
choices.D: the teaching given to borderline candidates is unusually poor

questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the two sets of candidates 'have received the same teaching for the same number of years, and are paid differently for decades', and concludes: 'If pay tracked what had been learned, discontinuities of this kind would not appear.'

wrong.A: The passage says nothing about the accuracy of examinations as measures; it uses the cut only because teaching is held constant across it.
wrong.B: Employers' ignorance is mentioned later as part of the signalling account, not as what the cut-off finding establishes.
wrong.D: Equal teaching on both sides of the cut is the whole force of the example, so the quality of that teaching is not at issue.

questions.stem: The finding about students who leave after three of four years functions in the argument as:

choices.A: a case where earnings move with the credential and not with the instruction received
choices.B: evidence that students who leave early were less capable before they enrolled
choices.C: a demonstration that the final year of a programme teaches more than the earlier ones
choices.D: an illustration of how poorly employers estimate the length of a programme

questions.explanation: The second paragraph notes that such leavers earn 'far closer to those who never enrolled than to graduates, although they have sat through three quarters of the instruction', and the fourth returns to the same student: 'Something was acquired by the three-year leaver. What was not acquired was the document.'

wrong.B: Nothing in the passage characterises the capability of leavers; the cut-off example is introduced precisely to hold capability close to constant.
wrong.C: The passage treats the missing year as a missing document rather than as unusually productive instruction, since measured gains accrue to leavers too.
wrong.D: Employers are never said to misjudge the length of programmes; they are said to be unable to observe capability.

questions.stem:
Which of the following does the author accept?

I. The credential is informative to employers.
II. Additional years of schooling raise measured literacy.
III. The earnings curve rises smoothly with time spent studying.

choices.A: I only
choices.B: I and II only
choices.C: I and III only
choices.D: I, II, and III

questions.explanation: I is accepted in the third and sixth paragraphs, where the signal is said to be informative and not arbitrary. II is the fourth paragraph's finding from changes in the law. III is denied in the second paragraph, which says earnings rise 'sharply at the completion of a credential rather than smoothly with time spent studying'.

wrong.A: This leaves out the measured gains in literacy and numeracy that the fourth paragraph reports for extra years imposed by law.
wrong.C: Statement III is the view the second paragraph's evidence is marshalled against, so it cannot be among the author's commitments.
wrong.D: Statements I and II are both accepted, but III contradicts the discontinuities on which the argument turns.

questions.stem: Suppose a country doubled the number of its graduates over a decade and found that the wage advantage of a degree was unchanged while the share of posts demanding one rose sharply. The author would most likely treat this as:

choices.A: consistent with the prediction he draws from the signalling account
choices.B: evidence that the instruction given to the new graduates was ineffective
choices.C: a result that neither of the two claims he distinguishes can accommodate
choices.D: grounds for concluding that the private return to a degree is now negative

questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph makes exactly this prediction: enlarging the supply of credentials 'mostly raises the level at which the signal is set, and each cohort must go further than the last to say the same thing about itself', with the rising share of posts requiring a degree given as the confirming figure.

wrong.B: The passage separates teaching from pay, so a stable wage gap is not treated as telling us anything about what the new graduates learned.
wrong.C: The result is the signalling claim's own prediction, which is why the author reports the trend as confirmation.
wrong.D: A high private return alongside a falling social return is what the fifth paragraph describes; nothing suggests the private return turns negative.

questions.stem: Which finding would most weaken the author's claim that a single figure for the value of a degree conceals two different things?

choices.A: Graduates in fields with licensing examinations earn more than graduates in fields without them
choices.B: Employers report that they use the degree mainly to reduce the number of applications they read
choices.C: The wage gap between graduates and non-graduates differs widely from one country to another
choices.D: Earnings rise in proportion to instruction received once the credential itself is held constant

questions.explanation: The author's distinction rests on the discontinuities: pay jumps at the credential and not with instruction. A result in which earnings move with instruction once the credential is fixed would show the two were never separable in the data, collapsing the distinction the sixth paragraph asks future studies to make.

wrong.A: Licensing would add another kind of credential, which the author's framework already accommodates rather than being embarrassed by.
wrong.B: Screening to reduce reading is the sorting function the author grants to the signal, so this supports rather than weakens him.
wrong.C: Cross-country variation in the size of the gap says nothing about whether the gap has two components, which is the claim at issue.

questions.stem: The main point of the passage is that:

choices.A: earlier societies took less interest in the welfare of their young than ours does
choices.B: childhood is a recently assembled category that bears the marks of its making
choices.C: governing by age should be replaced by judgements of individual capacity
choices.D: the protections societies extend to the young rest on a historical mistake

questions.explanation: The first paragraph announces that the category 'has a history, and the history is shorter than the assumption implies', and the fourth states the conclusion precisely: 'the category carries the shape of the instruments which made it'.

wrong.A: The second paragraph sets this reading aside at once as 'both false and beside the point'.
wrong.C: The last paragraph rules this out, noting that case-by-case judgement of capacity 'is the thing the registers were adopted to avoid'.
wrong.D: The fourth paragraph insists the protections 'are not fictions' and warns against reading the genealogy as a debunking.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the parish records and household inventories described the young primarily by:

choices.A: their relation to the household that had taken them in
choices.B: the trade to which their families intended to bind them
choices.C: the number of years that had passed since their birth
choices.D: what they were able to do and the position they held

questions.explanation: The second paragraph says those documents 'describe the young by what they could do' and concludes that in them 'Years lived mattered less than capacity and station'.

wrong.A: Household standing is one half of the criterion the passage gives, but the records are said to turn first on capacity, not on who had taken a young person in.
wrong.B: Binding to a trade appears as one example of a capacity the records noted, not as the organising principle of their vocabulary.
wrong.C: This is what the passage denies of those records, and the denial is the basis of the whole genealogy.

questions.stem: The author's insistence that the genealogy is not a debunking serves chiefly to:

choices.A: acknowledge that the historical record is too thin to support a stronger claim
choices.B: concede that the category may have existed earlier under a different name
choices.C: separate the claim that a category was made from the claim that it is false
choices.D: defend the schools against the charge of having invented the age-norm

questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph makes the distinction explicit: 'Showing that a category was assembled does not show that it is false, or that we would do better without it.' The developmental differences are then said not to be 'artefacts of the registers'.

wrong.A: No doubt is expressed about the records; they are used confidently, and the hedge concerns what follows from them rather than their quality.
wrong.B: The second paragraph says the reverse, that 'no single word in those records does the work our word does'.
wrong.D: The schools are credited with gathering pupils by birth year, and the passage neither charges nor defends them in that respect.

questions.stem: The three developments described in the third paragraph are alike in that each:

choices.A: was adopted for reasons unconnected with the category it helped produce
choices.B: was resisted by the households whose children it reclassified
choices.C: replaced an older threshold with one set at a higher age
choices.D: was introduced by a state seeking to count its population

questions.explanation: The paragraph opens by saying the three developments assembled the category with 'none of them intending it', and each is given a motive of its own: the graded class 'needs cohorts', the labour line used age because it 'could be read off a register', and records made age something the state knew.

wrong.B: No resistance by households is reported anywhere in the passage.
wrong.C: Only the labour regulation involves a threshold, and the passage says nothing about what age preceded it.
wrong.D: Counting is the motive of the third development alone; schooling and labour regulation are given different motives.

questions.stem: A court must decide how to treat a fifteen-year-old whose understanding of a contract is demonstrably that of an adult. The passage suggests that the difficulty the court faces is:

choices.A: evidence that the protections built around childhood were never justified
choices.B: a sign that the developmental findings of the schools have been overstated
choices.C: a predictable consequence of a line drawn by registers rather than by capacity
choices.D: a case the older vocabulary of capacity and station would also have failed to settle

questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph places such cases where its argument predicts them: institutions must 'treat the age as the fact and the capacity as the anomaly', and the disputes 'cluster exactly where one would expect them to cluster if the line had been drawn by registers'.

wrong.A: The author calls the protections real and warns that assembly does not imply falsity, so he draws no such conclusion.
wrong.B: The developmental differences are explicitly said not to be artefacts, and nothing in the passage questions them.
wrong.D: On the passage's account the older vocabulary turned on capacity, so a demonstrated capacity is what it would have gone by.

questions.stem: The author's account of how the modern category was assembled would be supported by all of the following discoveries EXCEPT:

choices.A: early labour statutes took their thresholds from ages already entered in registers
choices.B: graded classrooms appeared before any law had fixed a minimum working age
choices.C: parish clerks recorded a young worker's trade but not his year of birth
choices.D: the earlier records set the young off from adults at a fixed number of years

questions.explanation: The second paragraph's finding is that in those records 'Years lived mattered less than capacity and station'. A record that divided the young from adults by a fixed age would contradict the genealogy rather than support it.

wrong.A: This supports the account, which has the labour line drawn at an age 'because an age could be read off a register'.
wrong.B: This supports the ordering the third paragraph gives, in which the schoolroom was already standing when the labour line acquired its meaning.
wrong.C: This supports the second paragraph, where the documents describe the young by capacity and station rather than by years.

questions.stem: The passage is best described as an argument that:

choices.A: language instruction for newcomers should be replaced by instruction for employers
choices.B: second-generation newcomers adapt more completely than their parents everywhere
choices.C: rates of intermarriage are a poor measure of how far a group has adapted
choices.D: what is called assimilation is better explained as a result of acceptance than a cause of it

questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph states the inversion directly: 'Acceptance is not the reward for assimilation; what we call assimilation is largely the record of acceptance already granted.'

wrong.A: The last paragraph says instruction is not useless, 'since a language is worth having whatever it buys', and no programme for employers is proposed.
wrong.B: This is asserted in the third paragraph as a step in the argument, not as its conclusion.
wrong.C: Intermarriage is used as one of the measures the author relies on, so he does not treat it as a poor one.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the standard account treats acceptance as:

choices.A: something that follows from how far newcomers have adapted
choices.B: a condition that institutions grant before adaptation begins
choices.C: a variable that differs mainly across countries of origin
choices.D: an outcome that language classes have been shown not to affect

questions.explanation: The first paragraph summarises the standard account as holding that 'the degree to which they do so explains how well they come to be received', and then names the terms: 'Acceptance is the dependent variable and adaptation the independent one.'

wrong.B: This is the author's own inversion in the fourth paragraph, not the account he is describing in the first.
wrong.C: Variation across origins is one of the author's measurements, and he reports that it is smaller than variation across receiving regions.
wrong.D: The passage never reports a study of whether classes affect acceptance; it says a language is worth having in any case.

questions.stem: Suppose audit studies in one region found no penalty at all for applicants whose records showed local schooling. On the author's account this would most likely indicate that:

choices.A: the standard account holds in regions where schooling is locally provided
choices.B: audit studies cannot detect a penalty against applicants who were locally schooled
choices.C: adaptation explains acceptance once the country of origin is held constant
choices.D: that region admits newcomers more readily than the regions where the penalty persists

questions.explanation: On the inverted account what varies is the receiving institutions, since rates 'vary far more across receiving regions than across countries of origin', and the markers of adaptation 'do not purchase acceptance'. A region without the penalty is therefore a region that admits.

wrong.A: The schooling is the same in both kinds of region, so on the author's account the difference must lie in the region rather than in the schooling.
wrong.B: The studies are described as detecting penalties in exactly this population, which is how the finding in the third paragraph was obtained.
wrong.C: Holding origin constant is the author's own design, and it is what shows adaptation not to be the explanatory variable.

questions.stem: The author's treatment of religious communities that keep their practices while facing no penalty suggests that he regards such cases as:

choices.A: the strongest evidence yet produced for the standard account
choices.B: consistent with his account once two kinds of persistence are distinguished
choices.C: too rare to count against a claim supported by regional comparisons
choices.D: evidence that civic participation and endogamy are incompatible

questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph concedes the case and then draws the distinction: persistence under admission is 'selective rather than general, avowed rather than defensive, and unaccompanied by withdrawal from common institutions', and 'the two kinds of persistence separate cleanly on measures of civic participation'.

wrong.A: The author answers the case rather than conceding the standard account, and the standard account is not said to predict it.
wrong.C: He calls it 'the standing example' and meets it on the merits instead of dismissing it as rare.
wrong.D: The passage says the opposite: persistence under admission comes without withdrawal from common institutions.

questions.stem: Which finding would most strengthen the author's inversion?

choices.A: A region that opened its housing market saw language shift accelerate in groups already settled there
choices.B: Newcomers who completed civic instruction reported a stronger sense of belonging than those who did not
choices.C: Groups from one origin maintained their language longer than groups from any other origin
choices.D: Audit studies found smaller penalties in regions where newcomers were a larger share of the population

questions.explanation: The inversion predicts that admission to ordinary membership causes the markers of difference to 'lose their function and fall away without anyone being instructed'. A change in admission followed by a change in practice among people already present is that prediction tested in time rather than across regions.

wrong.B: This runs with the standard account, in which the migrant's adaptation drives how they are received and how they feel.
wrong.C: Variation by origin is what the author reports to be the weaker source of variation, so a result of this kind tells against him.
wrong.D: A correlation with group size says nothing about whether admission precedes the practices, which is the claim at issue.

questions.stem: The caution in the final paragraph is best understood as an admission that:

choices.A: the audit studies were not designed to measure belonging
choices.B: same-origin comparisons cannot be made across more than one decade
choices.C: the regions that admit newcomers may differ from others in ways not measured
choices.D: reported belonging is unreliable when collected from second-generation respondents

questions.explanation: The paragraph says regions 'differ in many ways besides their openness' and offers the specific alternative that 'a region that admits newcomers readily may also be the region whose labour market was expanding when they arrived'.

wrong.A: The audit studies are not what the caution concerns; it concerns the regional comparison that carries the main argument.
wrong.B: The decade is held constant in the comparison as a strength of the design, and no limit on its span is mentioned.
wrong.D: Reported belonging is used without qualification; what is qualified is the inference from regional differences.

questions.stem: The author's own account of a judgement such as shallow is that it:

choices.A: records a sensation the critic had, expressed in the language of description
choices.B: claims that a certain way of attending to the work will find something there
choices.C: predicts the verdict competent listeners will eventually come to share
choices.D: applies a standard of execution that the performance has failed to meet

questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph states it: the judgement 'claims that the performance rewards a certain way of listening, and it is answerable in the way directions are answerable, by being followed'.

wrong.A: The second paragraph eliminates the report of pleasure, noting that a critic may be bored by a performance she judges superb.
wrong.C: Consensus is eliminated in the third paragraph as 'evidence about a judgement of this kind' rather than what it is about.
wrong.D: Rules are the third candidate and are eliminated as either too coarse or derived backwards from admired performances.

questions.stem: The author rejects the view that a critical judgement reports the critic's pleasure partly on the ground that:

choices.A: being bored by a performance one judges superb involves no contradiction
choices.B: critics are trained to set aside whatever pleasure they take in a performance
choices.C: pleasure is too variable between listeners to be reported accurately
choices.D: audiences rarely agree about which performances they have enjoyed

questions.explanation: The second paragraph gives this as the first reason: a critic may be bored by a performance she judges superb and gripped by one she judges cheap, and 'in saying both she contradicts herself in no way at all'.

wrong.B: No claim about training or self-denial is made; the point is that the two reports are about different things.
wrong.C: Variability between listeners belongs to the consensus candidate, and the author does not argue from inaccuracy of report.
wrong.D: Audience disagreement is never discussed; the disagreement the passage cares about is the kind that 'goes somewhere'.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that a review consisting of a confident verdict and no account of where to listen is defective because it:

choices.A: conceals the pleasure that actually prompted the critic to write
choices.B: omits the instructions a judgement of this kind commits its author to giving
choices.C: appeals to a consensus the critic has no good reason to expect
choices.D: applies rules of execution without stating which rules they are

questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph says the critic 'incurs an obligation to say where to listen', and that a review offering 'a verdict and no route is not doing the thing even when its verdict is the one we would give'.

wrong.A: Concealed pleasure is not the complaint; the account has already set pleasure aside as the wrong report.
wrong.C: Appeal to consensus is a separate candidate account, not the defect identified in the bare verdict.
wrong.D: The objection to rules is that they cannot ground a judgement at all, so naming them would not repair the review.

questions.stem: Suppose two listeners follow a critic's direction to a particular transition and neither finds anything there. On the author's account, this would show that:

choices.A: the listeners lack the practice that criticism presupposes in its readers
choices.B: the judgement reported a pleasure that the critic alone had taken
choices.C: the critic had applied a rule that the performance never broke
choices.D: the critic's judgement has failed in the way a direction can fail

questions.explanation: The final paragraph provides for exactly this case: a claim about what rewards attention 'can fail as a direction fails: you follow it and the thing is not there'.

wrong.A: Taste is called a practice one can be better or worse at, but nothing in the case described points to incompetence rather than to a false claim.
wrong.B: The account of judgements as reports of pleasure is eliminated in the second paragraph and is not revived to explain failures.
wrong.C: Rules are eliminated in the fourth paragraph, and the critic in this case has given a direction rather than invoked a rule.

questions.stem: Which of the following would the author be LEAST likely to regard as a well-formed critical judgement?

choices.A: The reputation this recording has acquired will not survive another generation of listeners
choices.B: The slow movement is played as a single line, and the inner parts are left to look after themselves
choices.C: The ornaments are added so freely that the shape of each phrase is lost under them
choices.D: The opening is taken so fast that the arrival of the second theme passes without event

questions.explanation: On the author's account a judgement must point somewhere in the performance to be followed, and the third paragraph denies that eventual consensus is what such a judgement is about. A forecast about reputation gives a listener no place to listen.

wrong.B: This names a feature and tells the listener where to attend, which is the form the fifth paragraph requires.
wrong.C: This is a direction of the kind the author approves, identifying what attention will find and where.
wrong.D: This locates a specific passage and says what will be missing there, which satisfies the author's criterion.

questions.stem: The author's objection to grounding criticism in rules is that such rules are either:

choices.A: too demanding to be met or too easily met by inexperienced performers
choices.B: satisfied by performances nobody admires or extracted from ones already admired
choices.C: borrowed from other arts or confined to matters of technical execution
choices.D: disputed among critics or ignored by the performers they are meant to guide

questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph puts the dilemma in those terms: rules are 'either coarse enough to be satisfied by performances nobody admires, or they have been derived backwards from performances already admired, in which case they summarise a judgement rather than grounding one'.

wrong.A: Neither horn concerns the difficulty of meeting a rule, and the passage says nothing about inexperience.
wrong.C: The passage draws no comparison with other arts and treats fidelity to the text as one of the rules at issue.
wrong.D: Disagreement among critics belongs to the discussion of consensus, and performers' compliance is never raised.

questions.stem: The central claim of the passage is that:

choices.A: some of what is classed as faulty risk perception answers to a different question than the actuary's
choices.B: insurers should set premiums with the vividness of a loss as well as its frequency in view
choices.C: the studies of lay risk judgement have been undermined by their choice of hazards
choices.D: households would insure more sensibly if they were taught the arithmetic of pooling

questions.explanation: The third paragraph states the thesis: 'the quantity people are responding to is not the quantity the calculation produces, and the mismatch is not always a mistake', and the last paragraph keeps the programme while exempting the refusal to treat one's exposure as an average.

wrong.B: The second paragraph says an insurer pricing to perceptions 'would be insolvent within a few years', so this is the opposite of the author's position.
wrong.C: The author calls the findings strong, saying explicitly that his reason is 'not that the findings are weak'.
wrong.D: The closing paragraph denies that the refusal at issue is 'a failure to grasp the arithmetic', so instruction is not the remedy proposed.

questions.stem: The author distinguishes insuring a loss one could absorb from declining to treat one's exposure as an average in order to:

choices.A: show that the published frequencies are less reliable than they appear
choices.B: argue that households should carry larger deductibles than they choose
choices.C: explain why demand for coverage lapses in the years after a flood
choices.D: separate a judgement he grants is irrational from one he defends

questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says the findings 'lump together two judgements that ought to be kept separate', calling the first 'irrational on any reading' and the second not.

wrong.A: The second paragraph insists the frequencies 'are not a matter of opinion', so their reliability is not in question.
wrong.B: Deductibles are mentioned only as the small-loss case the author concedes; no recommendation about their size is made.
wrong.C: The lapse is handled separately in the last paragraph, where it is the error the author says nothing defends.

questions.stem:
Which of the following behaviours does the author consider genuinely in need of correction?

I. Buying coverage against a loss that savings would cover
II. Refusing to price one's own exposure at its expected value
III. Allowing flood coverage to lapse in the years after a flood

choices.A: I only
choices.B: I and II only
choices.C: I and III only
choices.D: I, II, and III

questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph calls I 'irrational on any reading' and the last paragraph names III among 'the errors worth attacking', saying 'nothing in the foregoing defends' it. II is what the same paragraph says 'should not be attacked'.

wrong.A: This omits the lapse of coverage, which the final paragraph singles out as the error it most wants attacked.
wrong.B: Statement II is the judgement the author defends, calling it 'a correct view about whose arithmetic it is'.
wrong.D: Statements I and III are errors by the author's lights, but including II contradicts his central defence.

questions.stem: The author's treatment of recency suggests that he regards a household's response to a recent flood as:

choices.A: a reasonable reading of local conditions, though a poor estimate of probability
choices.B: the one component of lay risk judgement that the studies have measured badly
choices.C: an error whose persistence shows how little published frequencies are read
choices.D: evidence that base rates should be published at the level of the street

questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph says in so many words that 'Responding to an event is a poor way to estimate a probability and a decent way to read a situation', after listing the local particulars no table of base rates contains.

wrong.B: The author says these are 'harder to defend' rather than badly measured, and he does not fault the studies' measurement.
wrong.C: Nothing is claimed about whether households read published frequencies, only about what such frequencies omit.
wrong.D: Finer publication is a remedy the passage never proposes; the argument concerns how to classify the response.

questions.stem: A regulator proposes to require that every policyholder be shown the expected value of the losses covered next to the premium charged. The author would most likely respond that the measure:

choices.A: would misstate the premium, since a premium includes the cost of carrying the risk
choices.B: should be resisted because expected values are estimates rather than established facts
choices.C: would correct the vividness effect that the studies of willingness to pay report
choices.D: would mislead where the covered loss is one the household could not recover from

questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph's objection applies directly: an expected value 'is a statement about a population of events' while 'A household faces one draw', and the two come apart 'precisely for the low-probability, high-severity events'.

wrong.A: The second paragraph gives the premium as expected loss plus carrying cost, which the proposal does not misstate; it simply shows one component.
wrong.B: The author treats frequencies as 'not a matter of opinion', so he would not object on grounds of uncertainty.
wrong.C: Vividness is the part of the literature the author declines to defend, and he claims no remedy for it.

questions.stem: The author would most likely agree that an insurer which refused to sell coverage against small and absorbable losses would be:

choices.A: responding to the vividness of such losses rather than to their frequency
choices.B: withholding a product that buyers have no good reason to want
choices.C: departing from the arithmetic on which the pooling of risks depends
choices.D: treating a household's exposure as an average rather than as one draw

questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph is explicit that 'Paying a loading to insure a loss one could absorb out of savings is irrational on any reading', so coverage of that kind is what the author thinks buyers have no reason to buy.

wrong.A: Vividness is described as a feature of how buyers respond, not of how an insurer prices or decides what to offer.
wrong.C: Pooling is said to work on frequencies, and declining to sell a particular policy does not conflict with that arithmetic.
wrong.D: Treating one household's exposure as an average is the move the author criticises, and refusing to sell small coverage is not an instance of it.

questions.stem: The central claim of the passage is that:

choices.A: distortion is an unavoidable cost that careful disclosure of the projection repays
choices.B: a map can be judged only once the question it was made to answer is settled
choices.C: maps of features that move should show the range within which they move
choices.D: cartographers have been reluctant to admit how many choices their work involves

questions.explanation: The third paragraph states it: 'accuracy is a relation between a map and a question, and a map cannot be checked until the question it answers has been fixed.' The river case is introduced in order to reach this claim.

wrong.A: The first paragraph treats this as the usual lesson and sets it aside for leaving 'the harder question untouched'.
wrong.C: The envelope of wandering is one of four defensible lines, each right for a different question, and the passage recommends none of them in general.
wrong.D: No claim about cartographers' candour is made; the fault discussed is a map that conceals its question, not a profession that conceals its methods.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the four defensible lines for a moving river are best understood as:

choices.A: four estimates of a single channel, differing in their margins of error
choices.B: four conventions among surveyors, none of which has prevailed
choices.C: four distinct quantities, each answering to a different use
choices.D: four stages of a channel, of which only the latest is current

questions.explanation: The second paragraph says of the four lines: 'These are not four competing estimates of one quantity. They are four different quantities, each the right one for a different question.'

wrong.A: This is the reading the passage explicitly rejects in denying that the lines compete as estimates.
wrong.B: Surveying conventions are never mentioned, and the lines are distinguished by use rather than by professional practice.
wrong.D: Only two of the four are channels at particular times; the envelope and the valley axis are not stages of anything.

questions.stem: The passage supports all of the following claims about the moving river EXCEPT that:

choices.A: a channel as surveyed may be accurate for a season and misleading afterwards
choices.B: a line drawn where the water has never run would be wrong on any reading
choices.C: the question a user brings to the sheet determines which line serves them
choices.D: the envelope of a century's wandering is the soundest of the available lines

questions.explanation: The second paragraph puts the four lines on a level as 'four different quantities, each the right one for a different question'. The envelope is named there as the line suited to a flood plan, not as the best line generally.

wrong.A: This is supported: the mapped channel 'is correct for a season' and then 'describes a dry bed'.
wrong.B: This is supported by the fourth paragraph, where such a map 'would be wrong on every one of them'.
wrong.C: This is supported throughout the second and third paragraphs, which match each line to a use.

questions.stem: The author describes the blank interior of a nautical chart primarily to show that:

choices.A: a map's purpose can be made plain by what it declines to include
choices.B: omissions are the most common source of error in navigational work
choices.C: charts are more rigorously produced than maps intended for general use
choices.D: readers routinely mistake an empty area for an area with nothing in it

questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph says the chart 'announces its question in its omissions' and is honest 'because its purpose is legible in what it leaves out'.

wrong.B: The omission is presented as a virtue of the chart, not as a source of error.
wrong.C: No comparison of production standards is drawn; the comparison is about whether the question is legible.
wrong.D: The passage says the opposite, that 'no one takes the blank interior for a claim that nothing is there'.

questions.stem: A transit map draws every line straight and spaces the stations evenly, so that no distance on it corresponds to a distance on the ground. The author would most likely judge this map:

choices.A: sound, because the question it answers is evident from how it is drawn
choices.B: faulty, because the distortion it introduces is nowhere declared
choices.C: sound, because riders are rarely interested in distances between stations
choices.D: faulty, because a sheet with no scale cannot be checked for accuracy

questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph's standard is that a map is honest when 'its purpose is legible in what it leaves out', as with the chart's blank interior; the fault the fourth paragraph names is answering 'a question it conceals', which a map drawn this openly does not do.

wrong.B: Declaring the projection is called 'a start' that 'tells a reader little'; the author's test is the legibility of the question, not a declaration.
wrong.C: The author's reasoning turns on what the map makes plain, not on what riders happen to want to know.
wrong.D: On the author's account a map is checked against its question, so the absence of a scale does not by itself put it beyond checking.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that a map can be judged only against the question it answers?

choices.A: Most readers of maps could not name the projection used on any sheet they own
choices.B: Charts of one coast drawn for different purposes agree about the depths they print
choices.C: Features that move are a small minority of those a national survey records
choices.D: Surveyors settle disputes about a sheet by remeasuring the ground, not by asking its purpose

questions.explanation: The third paragraph claims that 'accuracy is a relation between a map and a question, and a map cannot be checked until the question it answers has been fixed'. A practice of checking sheets without reference to their purpose would be a standing counter-example.

wrong.A: The fifth paragraph already says a note naming the projection 'on its own tells a reader little', so this agrees with the author.
wrong.B: Agreement about one quantity is compatible with the claim, since the author allows several sheets to be right for different questions.
wrong.C: The moving river is offered as a hard case from which the claim generalises, so its rarity does not bear on the generalisation.

questions.stem: The passage is primarily an argument that disputes about gifts should be understood as disputes about:

choices.A: the obligations a form of transfer creates rather than the intentions behind it
choices.B: the rules of etiquette that govern repayment in different societies
choices.C: whether givers are more often generous than they are calculating
choices.D: the kinds of goods that a society is entitled to put up for sale

questions.explanation: The third paragraph makes the move: the question 'is not about what a giver wants but about what the form of a transfer creates', after the second paragraph concludes that 'Whatever motives are doing, they are not doing the explaining'.

wrong.B: The asymmetries of repayment are explained by the account in the fourth paragraph; they are evidence for it, not its subject.
wrong.C: This is the quarrel about motives that the passage sets aside as misplaced from its first paragraph on.
wrong.D: Limits of exchange appear in the last paragraph as an application, and the author declines to settle the question they raise.

questions.stem: The experimental findings reported in the second paragraph are said to show that giving responds strongly to:

choices.A: the size of the return a giver has reason to expect
choices.B: whether the recipient is known to the giver beforehand
choices.C: how a giver describes his own reasons when surveyed
choices.D: the form in which a transfer is made and recorded

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports that giving is 'strongly altered by manipulations of form', listing the ledger, cash or kind, and the presence of others, while 'information about the likelihood of a future return changes them much less'.
