wrong.A: Expectation of return is named as the factor that changes giving much less, which is the point of the comparison.
wrong.B: Prior acquaintance between the parties is not among the manipulations the passage reports.
wrong.C: Respondents' descriptions of their own reasons are reported not to distinguish their patterns of giving at all.

questions.stem:
On the author's account, which of the following marks a transfer as a gift rather than a sale?

I. The transfer leaves the parties with something outstanding between them
II. The giver is not expecting anything in return
III. No sum or date attaches to what the recipient now owes

choices.A: I only
choices.B: I and III only
choices.C: II and III only
choices.D: I, II, and III

questions.explanation: The third paragraph distinguishes the two by closure: a sale leaves the parties 'quits', whereas a gift leaves 'a standing in a relationship which further transfers express', with 'no sum, no date and no enforcement'. II is rejected in the second paragraph, where motives are said not to do the explaining.

wrong.A: This omits the absence of sum and date, which the third paragraph gives as part of what distinguishes the recipient's position from a debt.
wrong.C: Statement II makes the giver's expectation decisive, which is the motive-based criterion the passage argues against.
wrong.D: Statements I and III are both the author's, but II belongs to the generosity view he displaces.

questions.stem: A guest brings a bottle of wine to a dinner and the host hands him its exact price in cash at the door. On the author's account, the offence lies in the fact that the host has:

choices.A: declined a transfer that was offered with no expectation of any return
choices.B: closed a relationship that the guest's gift had just left open
choices.C: revealed that the evening was a transaction rather than an occasion
choices.D: refused an obligation that no law could have enforced against him

questions.explanation: The third paragraph has it that 'A sale closes' while 'A gift does not close', and the fourth that to settle a gift is 'to propose that the relationship the gift opened be settled and brought to an end'. Exact payment at the door performs that closing.

wrong.A: What the giver expected is a matter of motive, and the second paragraph concludes that motives are not doing the explaining.
wrong.C: On this account the offence is structural rather than a revelation about anyone's view of the evening.
wrong.D: The passage says what the recipient holds 'is not a debt, since there is no sum, no date and no enforcement', so there is no such obligation to refuse.

questions.stem: A charity finds that donors give less when told exactly what their money will buy and when sent an itemised receipt. The author's account would most readily explain this by:

choices.A: the donors' suspicion that the charity's own motives are commercial
choices.B: the loss of the anonymity that makes giving in public rewarding
choices.C: the itemising, which closes the transfer in the way a sale closes
choices.D: the donors' reduced expectation of any return from the charity

questions.explanation: The third paragraph identifies the mechanism: 'Cash entered in a ledger converts a gift into a sale precisely because a ledger closes an account.' An itemised receipt is a ledger entry settling what was given against what it bought.

wrong.A: Suspicion about the recipient's motives is a reading of minds, which the passage argues does not do the explanatory work.
wrong.B: The presence of others is listed among the manipulations of form, but nothing in the finding described involves a change in who observes the gift.
wrong.D: Expectation of return is the factor the experiments found to matter much less than form.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if established, would most undermine the author's account?

choices.A: Givers in laboratory studies report no expectation of a return of any kind
choices.B: Societies differ widely in which transfers they refuse to let be bought
choices.C: Rates of giving and of return are unchanged when a transfer is entered in a ledger
choices.D: Lobbyists' gifts are condemned more severely where they have been openly recorded

questions.explanation: The relocation rests on the second paragraph's finding that giving is 'strongly altered by manipulations of form', and on the third paragraph's claim that cash in a ledger 'converts a gift into a sale precisely because a ledger closes an account'. If the ledger made no difference, the form would not be doing the work.

wrong.A: Reports of expectation are reports of motive, which the author has already set aside as not explanatory.
wrong.B: Variation between societies in what may be bought is consistent with a test that asks which transfers are not supposed to close.
wrong.D: The account explains the condemnation structurally and makes no prediction about how recording changes its severity.

questions.stem: The main point of the passage is that:

choices.A: literary omissions are best analysed on the model of a rest in a score
choices.B: an omission depends on expectations the text has built, not on the silence itself
choices.C: readers who supply missing motives are reading less carefully than they suppose
choices.D: critics have overstated how often writers achieve an effect by leaving things out

questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph states the account the broken analogy yields: 'An omission is not an element of the text but a relation between the text and an expectation the text has formed in a reader; the writer's material is not silence but the expectations that make a silence audible.'

wrong.A: The analogy is pressed in order to find where it fails; the third and fourth paragraphs turn on its breaking down.
wrong.C: Supplying a motive is described as what readers normally do, 'usually without noticing', and no charge of carelessness is made.
wrong.D: The author does not count successes or failures; he reanalyses what the success consists in.

questions.stem: According to the passage, one respect in which a literary omission differs from a musical rest is that the omission:

choices.A: is filled in by readers, who supply different things
choices.B: occupies no place that a reader could locate in the work
choices.C: cannot be produced deliberately by a writer who intends it
choices.D: is noticed by every reader who reaches the page

questions.explanation: The third paragraph gives this as the second of three differences: a reader meeting an unstated motive 'does not experience a gap but supplies a motive, usually without noticing, and different readers supply different ones'.

wrong.B: The second paragraph says the reverse, that the undisclosed thing 'occupies a place that can be located precisely'.
wrong.C: The passage treats the technique as deliberate and discusses how writers build the expectation it needs.
wrong.D: The first difference listed is precisely that such an omission is not perceptible to a reader who has not registered the rhythm.

questions.stem: A novelist devotes two hundred pages to a marriage, recording every small exchange, and then reports the husband's death in six words. On the author's account, the effect of those six words depends chiefly on:

choices.A: the reader's willingness to imagine what the novelist has not described
choices.B: the contrast between the brevity of the report and the gravity of the event
choices.C: the rhythm of disclosure the preceding two hundred pages established
choices.D: the restraint the novelist shows in refusing a scene he could have written

questions.explanation: The second paragraph locates the effect in a departure from an established pace, and the last paragraph names the source: the technique's 'real work was done earlier, in building the expectation the restraint then disappoints.'

wrong.A: Readers' willingness is said not to be enough: 'a text that has established no rhythm of disclosure will not produce the experience in any reader, however willing'.
wrong.B: Gravity alone cannot do it, since on this account an unprepared omission 'is simply a thing not mentioned'.
wrong.D: Restraint is called 'the conspicuous half' of the technique, not the half that does the work.

questions.stem: The author's account implies that a reader who finds significant withholding in a plainly written report has:

choices.A: identified an omission the writer did not intend but nonetheless made
choices.B: applied to the text a criterion the author takes from the musical case
choices.C: brought expectations the text itself did nothing to establish
choices.D: mistaken an unstated motive for a stated one

questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph names this as one of the two opposite failures: 'The opposite failure belongs to readers who arrive with expectations the text did not build, and hear withheld meaning everywhere.'

wrong.A: On this account an omission requires an expectation the text formed, so there is nothing for the writer to have made unintentionally.
wrong.B: The musical criterion is countable duration, and the passage does not ascribe its misuse to such readers.
wrong.D: Confusing a stated motive with an unstated one is not a possibility the passage raises.

questions.stem: Suppose it were shown that readers given only the final chapter of a novel reported the same sense of significant omission as readers who had read the whole. This finding would most directly threaten the author's claim that:

choices.A: a rest cannot fail to be a rest however badly it is played
choices.B: criticism has treated the withheld scene as the achievement
choices.C: different readers fill an unstated motive in different ways
choices.D: the effect requires expectations the earlier text has built

questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph rests the reply to the objection on exactly this: 'a text that has established no rhythm of disclosure will not produce the experience in any reader, however willing'. Readers who never met the earlier pages would be having the experience without the expectations.

wrong.A: The claim about rests concerns music and is not touched by a finding about readers of a novel.
wrong.B: That is a remark about critical vocabulary, which such a finding would leave standing either way.
wrong.C: Variation in what readers supply is a separate observation, and the finding as described reports a shared sense rather than its content.
